what_worked: Slide 2's upfront caveat box and the B2B pricing-not-scale decomposition on slide 9 are genuinely excellent.
fix_next: Recompute all category medians and Stripe revenue share against the frozen reference before presenting; several are off by 2–3×.
verdict: Outstanding framing and narrative undermined by multiple verifiable numerical errors across key slides.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1/2/3: total revenue stated as $133.8M vs reference $15.6M — either a different metric or a major error, but all downstream percentages are built on it so treated as internally consistent yet unverifiable against reference. Slide 2: '72 deliberately anonymised' vs reference 129 anonymous. Slide 3: top-10 share 50.6% vs reference 49.6%. Slide 7: Education median MRR $2,142 vs reference ~$2,435/12≈$203 (or $2,435 annual); Marketing $1,586 vs reference median $2,369.50 (annual); Analytics $1,294 vs reference $419 (annual) — medians appear to use a non-standard denominator or are simply wrong. Slide 9: Stripe carries 89.7% of revenue vs reference $13.5M/$15.6M = 86.7%. Slide 5: 109 zero-revenue companies vs reference 216 zero-revenue rows.

evidence.insight: Slide 9's B2B vs B2C customer-count parity with 5.7× MRR gap is a genuinely original decomposition. Slide 6 bubble chart reframes AI crowding vs revenue share effectively. Slide 11 pricing anomaly (near-identical multiples despite huge MRR gap) is decision-useful.
evidence.narrative: Clean five-act arc: universe → concentration → categories → monetisation → exits. Each slide advances the power-law thesis. Conclusion slide synthesizes five numbered takeaways that map back to earlier slides.
evidence.framing: Slide 2's 'Read this before you trust any chart' box is exemplary — declares no time dimension, self-selection bias, and disclosure gaps upfront. Consistent footer with caveats on every slide. Missingness flagged at point of use (e.g., 274 missing categories, 243 missing countries).
evidence.accuracy: Seven material discrepancies against the frozen reference: total revenue figure ($133.8M vs $15.6M) is the largest and cascades; anonymous count, top-10 share, multiple category medians, Stripe revenue share, and zero-revenue count are all off. Internal consistency is maintained but external accuracy is poor.
evidence.visual: Consistent dark theme with clear hierarchy. Lorenz curve (slide 3), log-log bubble chart (slide 6), growth histogram (slide 10), and box-plot multiples (slide 11) are well-chosen and annotated. Side stat panels aid scanning. No decorative clutter.

change_reason: Added total-revenue mismatch ($133.8M vs $15.6M reference) and zero-revenue count discrepancy (109 vs 216) as additional factual errors, raising count from 6 to 7. However, the $133.8M figure may reflect a different aggregation (e.g., lifetime or gross) not captured by the reference's 12-month total, so confidence is medium. Core dimension scores unchanged as the preliminary assessment correctly identified the pattern of strong presentation with accuracy problems.
